utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I first informed the parties that we continue to work under Rule 15 bis since Judge Nieto-Navia is still ill. Nevertheless, the expectation is that he would return in the beginning of next week so that we would not go over the limit of three days. Before I ask the Defence to call its next witness, I would first like to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session now. May I take it that the Defence is ready to examine its next witness, to call its next witness? Madam Usher, can you please bring in the next witness. Could the technicians take care that when the witness enters the courtroom, that the facial distortion will be effective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, good afternoon, Mrs. DP3, as we will call you. First, I inform you about the decision of the Chamber, that the protective measures that have been requested have been granted. That means that facial distortion is effective and we will use a pseudonym. Before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that the witness will be disconcerted by the fact that she can see only two Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the previous witness saw first the three Judges, and so he might have noticed a change. You might be a bit surprised that there are only two Judges where there are supposed to be three. One of the Judges is ill and for a limited period of time we may continue. Everything you say is recorded both video and audio and is written down so he will read every single word you will tell the Chamber. Ms. Pilipovic, is it you who is going to examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But with your leave, my colleague might want to ask some questions as well. Again, only upon your approval.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, in view of the fact that the Chamber has granted you protective measures, we will address you as DP3. And before I start examining you, I would like you to take a look at this document and tell us what you think of it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that all of this information is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to turn into private session so that the witness can give personal information about where she lived and worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, you told us about where you lived and where you worked. Can you tell me, please, how long did you stay in your job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: To be precise, my last working day was the 16th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why is it that you worked only until April 16? Has something happened to cause you to start working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Starting on Saturday, the 4th of April, and up until the 16th of April it was a security risk to go to work. Life wasn't normal. It wasn't as usual. So on the 16th I ceased going to work due to my personal safety concerns.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "starting on April 4th," can you tell us whether something happened that you were able to observe yourself, and that indicated that your safety was jeopardised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: On Friday, April 3rd, and the night into 4th April, Saturday, was Ramadan and there was a lot of shooting in town both in my neighbourhood and in other parts of town. It was very clear what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "it was clear what was going on," could you clarify that for us? What was actually going on and who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: This was something that all of us expected because we were told explicitly that once the Ramadan came, there would be shooting. However, this was not typical for Muslims. I was 32 at the time, and that was the first time in my life that I heard them shooting on their religious holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that that was something to be expected in view of the previous events, can you tell us whether in town, and in the neighbourhood where you lived, there was something else going on that indicated that shooting was to be expected? Were there any incidents prior to April 4th 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: I suppose that the event of March 1st is well known to everybody else, and there is no need to go into details regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. When you tell us that you ceased going to work on April 16th because your personal safety was jeopardised, can you tell us, whether in your neighbourhood, you noticed something that was unusual, that was not typical for that part of town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Well at that time, nothing was usual, nothing was typical, nothing was as it was before. The stores had been plundered, the organisations and companies stopped working. There were people with arms in the streets. Some of them had pistols. Some had rifles. It was a very chaotic situation. So nothing resembled a typical city life.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that there were armed people walking about town, can you tell us whether they were just individuals, or were those groups of people and can you tell us how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Well, on the way to my apartment, I would meet individuals, but I would also meet groups of two or three people. And that was something new for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your neighbourhood, do you know or did you personally observe that certain families were evicted from their apartments by armed people? What I am interested in --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please rephrase your question, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, did you see certain families being harassed by armed people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: After the shooting of that night, the one that I mentioned, so on April 4th, the situation in my neighbourhood was such that I believed that it was not good for my children to remain there. And the same is true for my acquaintances, for my family. All of them were leaving their neighbourhoods and going towards suburbs, towards New Sarajevo and Lukavica, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say they were leaving town do you know whether families were leaving other neighbourhoods in town due to such situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: My sister and her family left her house on foot, the house located in Pofalici with just one travelling bag. The same is true of my uncle and my aunt who left Hrasno and the other neighbourhood, the same applied to other acquaintances and friends of mine. They all believed it was unsafe for them to remain in their neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, can you tell me in your neighbourhood, what was the composition, ethnic composition, of the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood, the majority of the population was Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that people were leaving Pofalici and Hrasno neighbourhoods, can you tell us what was ethnic composition there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: The Muslims were in majority in Pofalici, and we all know what happened later on in Pofalici. Hrasno was also a Muslim neighbourhood. Alipasino Polje was also a completely Muslim neighbourhood. Svrakino Selo was also a Muslim neighbourhood. This is where my mother-in-law lived. So all of these people started leaving those neighbourhoods and going to the parts of town where there was a Serbian majority. This is how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, and this movement of population from one neighbourhood into another, did this, according to you, mean that people were trying to move into areas where there was a majority of people that were of same ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Yes, that is what we did. My children and I left our neighbourhood because we felt that our security was jeopardised and we were in fear for our lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who did you feel you were at risk from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: In view of the events of March 1st, and in view of the fact on that same weekend on Ramadan, a Serb policeman was killed by in New Sarajevo police station, by his Muslim colleague and the authorities did nothing regarding that, and again in view of the fact that there were armed people in the streets with Patriotic League insignia and there was shooting going on without any sanctions by authorities when there was plundering going on, then I guess all should be clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, after these events in town, the events that you just described to us did something else take place in your neighbourhood? Did you try to organise yourselves in a way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: It was clear to us that we had to change our lifestyle. The man attempted to organise patrols in order to protect their women and children. And then there was that murder in the police station, the one that I described, and all of this involved people that I knew, including my late husband, the best man at our wedding, our neighbours, my late husband's childhood friends.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I apologise, but I would like you to give brief answers to my questions. When you just told us that your late husband and the bast man from your wedding and friends took part in neighbourhood watches, are you trying to tell us that they organised themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Well, what else could they have done? The police wasn't doing its job. It wasn't prosecuting offenders, so what else was there for them to do?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, can you tell us, did the men in your neighbourhood go and report somewhere? How did they organise themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Well, a while ago I started telling you that the only proper place where they could go was the Territorial Defence in that neighbourhood where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us, "Territorial Defence," could you clarify what the Territorial Defence could offer to the men in your neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: An organisational structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "an organisational structure," can you tell us whether they received certain weapons or uniforms, or did they simply go and report to Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: In our country, all men of military age were members of reserve forces of the army or police. And all of them had their assignments, the places where they had to go and report. And they normally were regularly called to report for exercises, military reserve exercises. All of them also had -- were issued uniforms that they normally kept at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, you told us that all of them had reserve forces uniforms, regardless of their ethic origin. Are you telling us, in fact, that men of all nationalities in your neighbourhood were organised in Territorial Defence or was the situation different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Territorial Defence was an organisation. It existed even in April of 1992, and at that time, everybody reported there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that in the part of town where you lived, in the Territorial Defence there were Serbs, Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: At that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, "at that time, yes," was that the case throughout the conflict? Was it in 1992, 1993, 1994, or did something happen which was different to what you just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: When we are talking about the period mid-April, from then on it was clearly defined, territorial in every way, who's on whose side. The city was divided.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was clearly defined territorially as well, and that whose side was which, and that the city was divided, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: For instance, specifically, for this part of town that I was, there was a majority Serb population and there was the Serb population, Serbian inhabitants who had arrived from other parts of town. And that means that they stayed there. So that is how it was, that is how it was in Ilidza. There were people who were there from before. Then there was the Novo Sarajevo municipality where I was. So these young men didn't go to Bascarsija or Hrasno or Pofalici. They stayed where their houses were, where their families were. And throughout, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would be grateful for the opportunity to raise an issue in private session, if I could. I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It would probably be better in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like the escort, the usher, out of the courtroom. We will ask you to leave the courtroom just for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think the estimate for this witness is approximately two hours in chief which means that we may get to cross-examination tonight. The Defence was required to provide to the Prosecution the names of witnesses and clearly, it is anticipated by all that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I am sorry. I forgot that we had to turn into private session. So we were not. But until this moment, I don't think that there are any accidents that happened. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated again. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before we had a break in the examination-in-chief, you were telling us about the situation in the part of town where you lived. You said that in your opinion, the city was divided. Did you continue to live in that part of town? Did you stay there, you and your husband, and your children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: With the children we went to the part of town, municipality Novo Sarajevo. It is a suburban part of town and it is in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that you went to another part of town with the children, are you telling us that you no longer lived in that part of town and in the street - please don't mention the street - or did you continue to live there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: It was -- there was no security. It was not possible to live safely in that street in that part of town with the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that your husband also went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: My husband, as I already said, went to report to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether your husband, as member of Territorial Defence, did he have any specific tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: He was an ambulance driver.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that he was an ambulance driver, could you tell us if your husband as an ambulance driver, did he have certain duties, and was he on duty in certain locations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: We were -- when I say "we" I mean women, children and the elderly, we were in this village in houses, and they, the men that is, had their positions in the watches, the guards, the patrols. That is what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that they had their positions in the guards and the patrols, were there any incidents at that time in that part of town? Is there anything that was happening at the time that wasn't usual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: There was sporadic shooting coming from all directions. Everyone knows that. That is what was also reported in the media, and we could hear it ourselves. So it was a situation which stopped being peacetime, a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge, and we are talking about April 1992 were there any important incidents where there were also casualties, wounded? Do you know and do you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Well, the worst thing that happened to me was the morning of the 21st of April 1992 in the early hours of the morning. I had already got up. That was 4.00 in the morning at dawn. I was awoken by horrific shooting and it was quite clear that there was combat activities going on. And in the morning, at about 7.00, at that time, we still had telephone lines that were operating. I called my neighbour from the -- from my building, and I asked her what was happening. She literally told me that there were many dead people in the street. The news reported that morning that the building Unioninvest was on fire. That day on the morning, I learned that my husband had been killed. He was driving the ambulance and he went -- drove to the Belgradska Street to get a person that was wounded, a wounded man.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that the media reported on that day, 21st of April 1992, that there were combat activities, and that the Unioninvest building was on fire, did you learn who were these clashes between? What were the sides in the combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: It was clear that the Serb forces were on one side, and that on the other side of Miljacka river, on the other side of town. These were the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn, considering that that's when your husband was killed, did you find out whether on the side of the Muslim forces, were there some Special Forces or was it Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: All the information that I ever got, and there was much that I got from the people who were there at the time, was that the forces of Vikic, Commander Vikic, forces at that time were--

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. President. This is evidence which is hearsay, and I appreciate that hearsay is not prime facie inadmissable but it relates to the incident of this witness's husband's unfortunate death, and she wasn't present at that. It is essentially at least it would seem secondhand hearsay, if not even further removed from that. And therefore, in my respectful submission, it is of little assistance to the Trial Chamber if the relevance of it is to attribute responsibility for the death of the witness's husband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, would you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is to be expected that the witness was able to find out what happened. But considering that in this operation, in this combat, this fighting, her husband was killed, it is to be expected that the witness certainly learned information that would be best possible information regarding their accuracy. So she found out about it. And we believe that the witness obtained the information and that she had checked them, and that they are accurate, regardless of the fact that she wasn't at the scene of the incident. You will understand that we did mention that she wasn't there. This is only what she heard. But considering there was combat and there were official announcements and there were also -- there is also information in the media. And the information that she got must be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your last remark is a conclusion. There are two issues. The first one is the -- whether this hearsay would be admissible, of any assistance, and the second issue is the relevance. May I urge you to keep both in mind. Until now, what we heard about the sources was of a very general nature. And I don't think that the Chamber, even keeping in mind the specific circumstances, could just assume, on the basis of these specific circumstances, that what the results of the findings were, without knowing in great detail about the source of knowledge, that it must have been true what the witness found out. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, who told you that in the operation and in the fighting that took place on the 21st of April that Vikic's units was involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Do you mean the names of the people who told me about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you do not wish to tell them the names in public --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we can go, Your Honour, in closed session so that the witness could tell us who told her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first ask you: Do you know the names of those who told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These people were, at the time, at the scene where my husband was and these were the people who got my dead husband out from where he died.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question is whether you know their names. If you say, for example, these were colleagues of my husband, I don't know the names, then it is no reason to turn into closed session. If you say I know the names, but I would rather not tell them in public -- but first I would like to know, do you know the names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know the names of at least three people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we will turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is confirmed on my screen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you left your apartment in April. Did you go back to that part of town and to your apartment after your husband was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: I went back to the apartment occasionally to take necessary things for myself and for my children. And I went to Grbavica to work, to the building, at that time this was a building called Mis and this is where authorities were in that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us did you and until when did you stay at that place of employment in that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Specifically in that building, we remained until - possibly - until the end of October 1992 and because of -- it was unsafe, the building we were often fired at, there was a flat roof, and the offices moved to the premises, the ground floor premises of the forestry faculty which is also in Grbavica, in the immediately vicinity of that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you left the offices where you had worked because it was unsafe. Could you tell us when that was, and what contributed to these conditions? First tell us when that was when when did you leave the premises?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: I first told you that we left at the end of October, but we did interrupt our work on a daily basis. There would be an attack, shooting would start. There would be bullets falling on the roof. And, of course, we would scatter wherever we could. So it would happen that on one particular day we wouldn't continue work sometimes, a few hours would pass, and then we would go back to work. So we never knew when the date of employment when we started of work, if it would be finished at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this evidence on the basis of relevance. It is not apparent to me at all the relevance of evidence of firing at buildings, civilian or otherwise, occupied by civilians or otherwise, on the side of the confrontation lines controlled by the forces of the Bosnian Serb army. That is not relevant to the counts in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the testimony and the answer of the witness, we believe that it is relevant. Because there witness spoke about her place of employment, about the part of town where she says there was daily shooting. So, I believe that Mr. Ierace stopped the testimony and our examination-in-chief at the time when the witness had already answered. And as the Defence was going to ask another question following from the witness's answer. But the witness herself said in her answer that this building where she had worked and where she had left -- she said they left because it was unsafe. I asked her why was it unsafe and she said there was daily shooting. So I don't know from which part of town and who had fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, Ms. Pilipovic, when I do understand the Prosecution well, that it is not in dispute in whenever way that there was regular shooting, especially in that period of time in areas where people, we are not talking about whether they were civilians or not, were working. So you, until now, took a lot of effort to establish something, as you just explained it to us, which is not contested by the Prosecution. So, therefore, you said you would just go now to another -- to some other questions. May I just ask Mr. Ierace if the next question would be whether the firing coming from the other side of the confrontation line, would that be contested, if the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question would be contested, Mr. President. We are talking about territory on the Bosnian Serb army side of the confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I don't see any relevance in that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are not saying this did not happen and whether it came from the other side of the confrontation lines would even, if true, would still be irrelevant in your view?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, it is not contested that there was regular firing at -- in the place where the witness lived or worked. Please keep that in mind when you continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us at which -- what was your employment. Could you tell us, you, as a person who is competent considering your profession and your job description, could you tell us what was necessary in order to issue a death certificate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Yes, I can. The fact of death of any person in legal terms, in legal procedure, is always proved by death certificate. Except from the register of dead people. In order to issue this certificate, certain public documents are needed. First of all, the main document would be the relevant birth certificate, then a marriage certificate, and a document that would prove the identity of that person, that would mean a document with a photograph. And also of the person who is reporting this fact to the authorised organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, having answered my question, what is necessary to issue a death certificate for a person who had died, and you said also that confirmation is needed. What does it entail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: It is a public document which, in its contents, tells about the personal details of the person who died, the deceased, date of birth, cause of death, and the most important, signature and seal of coroner and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the person who has to be a medical physician who has certified, established the death of that person. So that would be authorised doctor, authorised physician, who is authorised to issue such confirmation,

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you accept a confirmation of death as a document, as a valid document, if it did not have a seal and a signature of the physician of the coroner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: No. I would not be authorised to enter information into the registry of dead persons if the document was invalid.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we would now like to show to the witness document P738. These are death certificates, and they have been marked as A, B, C and D. The Defence has a number of these documents, but we don't know the exact chronological order of them. But with your leave, we would show these to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are these exhibits already admitted into evidence, Ms. Pilipovic, or are these new exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. These are exhibits of the Prosecution, P738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please next time indicate beforehand, at least to the Registrar, I don't know whether the Prosecution was informed about it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No. Nor it is referred to in the summary, no reference to it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, the mere fact that an exhibit has already been admitted into evidence does not take away your duty to inform the other party and the Registrar, that you will present that document to a witness. So it is -- would you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It was just a matter of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That worked against the Defence, in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is why we were unable to prepare this in advance. I think that with your leave it would be sufficient just to show this to the witness so that she can just take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to get it clear. You just mentioned a number. Did you retrieve the document, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it is possible that the document is numbered P3738?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I said, P3738, P.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It appears under a different number in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at some stage, I have an objection to this line of questioning. I would like to be heard on that very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would like to make that objection now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The evidence is that the witness became a registrar of the department of social services three months after her husband was killed. It is not at all clear to me what expertise that gave her to comment on death certificates issued by authorities on the other side of the confrontation line, in war conditions. In particular, how they authorises or equips her to comment on the sufficiency of death certificates produced in those circumstances. Secondly, the relevance, I take it is to whether certain individuals were killed. It is not clear from the question so far for what purposes the death certificates are said to be complete or incomplete. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, especially on the last issue, what is it that the Defence wants to establish, that death certificates were irregularly given or that the person who was on the death certificate might not have died, or what is the aim of this exercise? What do you want to establish? If you should tell us in the absence of the witness because it might influence the statement, please do so. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in view of the fact that this witness had a job of registrar, we wish to submit that the Defence doesn't know whether the people mentioned in the death certificates brought here by the Prosecution are alive or dead. All we are trying to do is challenge the authenticity of these documents because the Defence was pointing or challenging this before, while the Prosecution presented its case, because these documents lacked a seal and a signature that are required. The Defence believes this to be a very relevant item, and this is why we are bringing this up with this witness. We can also put the following question to this witness: We can ask her whether the work procedure for registrars was uniformed for the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina or was it different for certain parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you, Ms Pilipovic -- let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you asked the witness whether a death certificate could be given if it was not -- if there was not a signed and sealed document underlying it. So if documents have been accepted into evidence, it is of no use to give it to this witness. I mean, everyone, I take it could see whether there are signatures or seals on it. So it might be clear that, in the view of this witness, but I would just like to have a look at the document you wanted to show to the witness because then I would have a better --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, could you please confirm the letter associate would the number of the document? Was it 3738A?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is A, B, C, and D. One of these documents. Whichever one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the Chamber thinks it is of no use to ask this witness to establish that there is no seal or no signature of doctor on these documents. I think we went through these documents in quite some detail. And the Chamber is of the opinion that it would not add very much, that other persons who would come to the same conclusions as to the content of these documents. So, therefore, would you please come to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I have another request both to you and to you, Mrs. DP, could you please make a short pause between every question and answer because every word you say has to be translated. You are speaking the same language. It goes a bit too quick for the interpreters. If you would just wait until after the answer. It may be of help if you look at your screen. When you see as soon as the text stops moving, then you see it is up to you to answer. Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us about the building where you worked. Now, can you tell us this: Did you have to travel, and if so, how long from the apartment where you lived to your place of work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: I walked, and the time I needed varied due to what was going on while I went to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you had to pass through a settlement on your way to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Yes. I went through residential areas. There was shooting going on daily. It was very risky and difficult to move about. And we had to use special passages and special locations to get to other parts of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you had to use special passages and special routes, could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the simple issue is this: What has this evidence got to do with the charges against General Galic? This is the reason that we filed the tu quoque application, motion. Whether or not there was firing in the civilian areas of the territory controlled by the Bosnian Serb army is of no assistance to the Trial Chamber in determining whether the accused was ultimately responsible for sniping and shelling of civilians on the other side of the confrontation line. If we hear hours or weeks of months of this sort of evidence, it will not assist the Trial Chamber in determining those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has pointed out that we are not going to use or rely on tu quoque principle as a defence for General Galic, but bearing in mind the content of the indictment which has count 2, which goes on to say that the Serb forces in and around Sarajevo blocked the town and took strategically important locations, positions. Therefore, count 2 of the indictment says that in and around Sarajevo important strategic positions had been taken. We are now referring to the part of the town in which this witness resided. My learned friend said today that the Prosecution doesn't dispute that there was fighting going on in that part of town. The other count of the attack pertains to campaign and it says that the Sarajevo Romanija Corps had a campaign of daily shelling and sniping of certain parts of town. The Defence wishes to prove that there was no campaign going on. There was not a strategy of campaign there either, but there was a conflict, a combat going on in a certain territory, that it involved two sides and that in this specific part of town, there was daily shooting going on. Now, who was behind this shooting is not relevant, but it is evident that there was combat going on, and we do not know who and where did the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: -- If it is not clear yet to the Defence, I make it abundantly clear, that it is common ground that there was fighting, if not on a daily basis, then certainly on a regular basis, in Grbavica and other areas along the confrontation line. And therefore, this evidence is not needed in order to paint the background to the Prosecution case or the Defence case in that respect. In my respectful submission, there is a danger that if the evidence is not confined to the issues which are legitimately in dispute, then it will unnecessarily protract the trial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, if the Chamber understand the position of the Defence well, then it would be that, first of all, there was on a daily basis, at least very regular fighting, and certainly the area of Grbavica not being excluded. The second observation I would like to make is that the Defence has indicated that it will not use tu quoque as an argument but perhaps self-defence. So, there is as such no reason to establish the regular combat activity unless there would be a direct link between this combat activity and what is the Defence case, that is, either there was stray bullets or errors. I would say that would be in the context of a combat situation in certain areas which is not contested, as such, by the Prosecution; or that this fighting would have specific significance in respect of self-defence defence. So self-defence defence. So the Chamber cannot say that it is under all circumstances irrelevant that combat was going on but the mere fact that there was regular combat is not relevant as such. And apart from that, it is not contested. So if you would please indicate if you want to continue on this line of questioning, what the specific relevance is in view of the case of the Defence, then you are entitled to do so. And otherwise, I would like to ask you to move to your next subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has already explained why this type of questioning is relevant, especially in view of the indictment which claims that there was a campaign and a strategy of sniping and shelling from the positions taken by the Army of Republika Srpska. Therefore, strategic positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you a question: Even if there would be regular attacks by whenever weapons on the Grbavica area, would that mean that there could be no campaign -- I am not defining at this very moment what a campaign exactly would be -- but would the one exclude the other?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we are specifically referring to the area of Grbavica. But in addition to that, the Defence will prove that there was combat going on in all parts of town and the surrounding area. Therefore, in all parts of town where there was a separation line. So not only Grbavica, but also Mehurici, and Ilidza, and Hadzici and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Is that contested by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not contested by the Prosecution, so there is no need to establish that because the parties agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I was putting questions to the witness, and I think my last question for her was, which route did she take to work. She said that she went through residential areas, that she took special passages and areas that were protected. And this goes to prove, in Defence's view, that not only the combat and demarcation lines were in and around Sarajevo, as the Prosecutor claims, but that there was combat going on in all parts of towns. There were parts of town where streets were demarcation lines. As we said in our opening speech, there was even combat going on between two buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that contested by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No Mr. President. And I can think of an example in the Prosecution case in Dobrinja where we said that the part of the building was occupied by the SRK and another part of the same building by Presidency forces. So it is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is not in dispute, Ms. Pilipovic, so there is no need to establish something that the parties agree upon. Please proceed, but as I said, if the parties agree, I specifically ask again and again to the Prosecution, whether it is in dispute, and I think as a matter of fact the interpretation of these facts is a different matter. But the interpretation of facts, of course, is not a subject that could be easily dealt with by witnesses of fact. Of course, experts might give opinion on facts that both parties agree upon. But witnesses of fact, if I may stress it in this way, usually cannot, I would not say never, but usually could not assist in the interpretation of facts and especially in the interpretation of facts that they have not seen by themselves. Would you please keep this in mind when you continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wish to say that the witness believes that fact witnesses, there were people who were present in combat locations and location where there was shooting going on are the witnesses whose veracity cannot be disputed. We believe that expert witnesses will also support this. We were able to listen to the Prosecution witnesses for the past six or seven months who were fact witnesses and testified about directions of fire, without establishing whether one side or the other was behind such firing. We believe that there are fact witnesses who were daily present in certain streets and in buildings and locations, and who are able to tell us, to give us facts that are relevant for this Trial Chamber and for the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am not saying that your witnesses will not be able Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to give relevant facts, but the facts you want to establish at this very moment - we have asked what you wanted to establish - are not in dispute. So I would say they are already established. At least between the parties there is no disagreement as to the existence of these facts. But whatever new facts, new relevant facts you would like to establish, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before I proceed with examination, I would like the Prosecution to tell us whether they accept the fact that other parts of town which were under control of the Army of Republika Srpska, and specifically we will be talking about Grbavica Nedzarici, Ilidza, Hadzici, Ilijas, Vogosca whether people there had specific routes they had to take protected passages and routes in order to protect themselves from daily combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is an issue which is not relevant to the indictment. It is not relevant whether or not there were safe passages operating for civilians on the side of the confrontation lines controlled by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence believes that this is relevant because the Prosecution claims that there was a campaign behind all of this. This is an argument that supports the campaign mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have some difficulties in following you. Two questions: Perhaps the first one to the Prosecution, is it the interpretation of the Prosecution that the safe routes and perhaps concrete slabs or sheets hung in streets, is that evidence in support the campaign or is it evidence that would support the frequency of possible attacks on those who would have to pass there? Is it frequency or is it more? Is it that the Prosecution says if there are concrete slabs, then it must be a campaign, or is it just to say well there has been a reason to erect these concrete slabs or to hang these sheets that indicates that with some frequency that people fear that they might be fear if these protective measures were not have been taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I understand the question, Mr. President. The Prosecution case is that the existence of those anti-sniping measures or barricades that were erected on the Presidency side of the confrontation line were erected in order to reduce the risk of civilians being wounded and killed by fire emanating from the Bosnian Serb Army side of the confrontation line. So the facts that the Prosecution has sought to prove by that evidence are that civilians were wounded or killed in those locations by fire coming from the BSA side of the confrontation lines. Secondly, that the election of the barricades reduced the number of deaths and other forms of casualties, thereby allowing an inference that indeed fire had been coming and continued to come effectively to a lesser extent from those same sources. That evidence allows a further inference in conjunction with other evidence that the shooting was part of a campaign. So ultimately, it contributes to an inference that there was, in fact, a campaign of sniping and shelling civilians. Mr. President, the evidence, as I understand it, the Defence wishes to call goes to whether there were similar measures taken by civilians on the other side of the confrontation line. If one hypothetically, and I stress that word, assumes for the sake of the argument that civilians did those things on the other side of the confrontation line, and for the same reason, in other words, to minimise their exposure to deadly fire from the side of the confrontation line controlled by the Presidency army, that fact would, in my respectful submission, be irrelevant to the issues before this Trial Chamber because this is not an inquiry into what happened in Sarajevo. It is a hearing of evidence against the accused. And, therefore, it is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you stressed several times that you would need this evidence because it would demonstrate that there was no campaign. Could you please clarify that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we and the witnesses wish to prove that there was no campaign, but that during armed combat, two armies were opposed in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere. The translation says that "you and the witnesses want to prove." May I take it, if this is a correct translation, that it is a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check with my colleague, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is on page 65, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for technical reasons I will take over. We wish to prove through the testimony that is how this should be understood, and I would also like to say that there is another interpretation error, an important, BSA was read by the French booth, both sides. So this is wrong. This is what I wanted to say. Now, the reason I take over is to say the following, Mr. President, is that the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, Ms. Pilipovic was argue a certain issue. I asked for a clarification on a certain issue. I would like lead counsel to answer my question and then, of course, if there is anything that should be added by you, you could ask permission to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I suggest that the discussion continue in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I am wondering if we could do that, although it is of a general nature -- apart from that, we are about to have a break. I would like to give the opportunity to answer to my question, after the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom, we will continue, Mrs. DP after approximately 20 minutes, but I will ask at this very moment you to be escorted out of the courtroom. Madam Usher, would you please assist Mrs. DP3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your leave, I would just ask for a few seconds to clarify a couple of points, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would invite Ms. Pilipovic first to complete the beginning of the answer she was giving to me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite. We just need a few seconds to talk with the Ms. Pilipovic -- I was asking between us. I didn't want to address the Chamber. I just wanted to check with Ms. Pilipovic to check the transcript to confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of the things I would like to prevent to happen, is that if counsel is arguing a certain issue that if co-counsel thinks that at very moment that he has got better ideas, that he would interrupt and to take over. That is a situation I would like not to happen. We will adjourn until 6.00, and I will hear the answer from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you certainly are able to answer the question, I take it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If I understood my learned colleague correctly, my learned colleague says that the special routes, that is, passages, screens in certain parts of town in Sarajevo under the control of the BH Army were set up at certain locations because there was a campaign by the SRK in order to shoot in certain places. Now the Defence's response is -- sorry, the Prosecution says that it is not contested that there was screens on the other side, there were other routes, passages, and certain location where there was protection for civilians to pass through these places. What the Defence wish to prove that on the other side there were routes, locations, where citizens, civilians had to pass. Therefore, in this situation, we say, and we will prove, that soldiers and the Army of the SRK were operating as in self-defence. Yes, there was shooting in certain places, and in those places there was shooting on both sides. But we will prove that we, in certain places, in operating -- towards certain directions, were operating in self-defence. If there was wounding and if there was some firing causing injury of people passing in certain locations, this was the consequence of a war risk and not a consequence of a campaign, as the Prosecution claims. The Defence is aware of the fact that the Prosecution is not claiming that the BH Army was operating -- and I am specifically talking about Grbavica -- that there was a campaign of Muslims and their army towards the positions of the Republika Srpska Army on the other side. But we will say and we will prove that in certain locations there were -- there was combat and that combat was always a consequence of the Republika Srpska Army acting in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you have answered that question. Perhaps it raises even more questions than it is in answer to my question, such as the fact that they were acting in self-defence, would that exclude a campaign, that would be a question. You said it was rather war risk and not a campaign. Would a campaign exclude the existence of war risks? Well, you could raise a lot of questions in this respect. It also very much depends on the concept of self-defence you would use, how abstract it would be, how concrete it would be. The existence of such measures for self-defence cannot be regarded as under all circumstances irrelevant. So, therefore, you may put some questions to the witness, but let's not forget that, in general terms, the existence of combat in those areas is not in contest. And I think for the defence of self-defence, it certainly would not be necessary to know every single sheets throughout the city in all municipalities or concrete slabs. So ask the witness about facts in this respect, any relevance is not necessarily absent. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness is brought into the courtroom, the Defence would like to bring up a problem in relation to witnesses. Witness DP3 has been here since Monday waiting to testify. And the Defence has a problem that the witness has to return tomorrow because that is how the travelling schedule has been set up. We did not expect the debating to go on for so long and we didn't realise that the witness -- we expected the witness to be only testifying today. And it is obvious that we will not finish the testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Defence was making a schedule, we were doing it according to the time that the Defence needed because we did not know how much time the Prosecution is going to need for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. Madam Registrar, I am looking at you, is this courtroom tomorrow morning used?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has to leave tomorrow morning early, the witness -- sorry, the witness has to leave tomorrow morning early. There is just only one plane in the morning. We were just told that by the witness and victim unit. And I will just have one more question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's just see how far we come. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, before we had the interruptions, during the examination you said that you used certain routes when you were leaving your work to go home. Could you tell us, why did you use these routes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP3
utterances.text: Civilians had to use certain marked routes, there were screens, in order to protect them from sniper fire. From the side of the city, of course, there were places where you couldn't have protection at all because of the ground, the terrain, specifically, in the area of Lukavica where from Mojmilo hill there was daily roving fire and it was that the fire was directed on to a populated location.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the examination-in-chief has ended. I will just check whether my co-counsel has anything to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mrs. DP3 you will now be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I prefer to start off in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will turn into private session and I see that we are in private session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Especially because everyone is entitled to know that I apologise both for the interpreters and the technical staff that I didn't ask their consent when we took nine minutes' time extra. We will adjourn until tomorrow morning and we will then deal with any documents that we have to deal with. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 7.09 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 11th day of October, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
